events.title: AI writes my code just fine. It still couldn't draw one person.
events.summary: A solo developer in South Korea, writing code with heavy AI assistance for a party-game app, found that AI tools could help with code but could not draw an acceptable human character, so they removed the face from a pose-copying game.

events.title: Drawing a labelled overlay on a user photo with SVG (no canvas, no library)
events.summary: A developer post describes a framework-free SVG technique for drawing labelled overlays on user-uploaded photos when an AI model returns coordinates, using a palm-reading web app's three named curves as the example. It focuses on common display bugs such as misplaced boxes, overlapping labels, and drift on resize.
events.why_it_matters: For teams shipping AI features that annotate user images, the post highlights that coordinate-to-display mapping is a frequent source of visible defects even when model output is correct. It offers a practical, dependency-free approach to rendering labels accurately across devices and responsive layouts.

events.title: Hackers Steal About $2.7 Million From Polymarket Traders via Hijacked DebugBear Script
events.summary: A supply-chain attack against prediction market Polymarket replaced a third-party page-speed script on its website with malicious code, which sold some signed-in traders' positions and drained their funds on October 29. The company says it will refund roughly $2.7 million to 726 affected wallets, and blockchain records show stolen crypto of about $2.64 million reaching the attackers.
events.why_it_matters: The incident shows how a compromise of a third-party script can be used to attack a site's authenticated users directly, not just deface or surveil. Web teams loading external scripts on pages handling financial sessions should treat those suppliers as part of their attack surface and lock down what can execute in the browser.

events.title: Remove Watermarks Without Uploading: How We Built an In-Browser AI Editor
events.summary: A project called ClearPix has released a browser-based AI tool that removes watermarks from images by running its models entirely on the user's device, so files are not uploaded to a server. Its watermark-removal component is described as MIT-licensed and available on GitHub.
events.why_it_matters: This is a freely and openly available tool whose stated purpose is stripping watermarks from images, which has implications for creators and for anyone relying on watermarks to mark ownership. The local-browser design also reduces the privacy risk of uploading images to third-party services.

events.title: Inside Prefab UI’s Sandbox Escape: The Chain Behind CVE-2026-120338
events.summary: A critical sandbox escape has been described in Prefab UI's Generative UI feature, which runs caller-supplied Python code under Pyodide (Python compiled to WebAssembly) inside a Deno subprocess. Although the sandbox is documented as isolation for untrusted code, a chain defeats it, tracked as CVE-2026-120338.
events.why_it_matters: The flaw is rated critical with a CVSS score of 10.0, the maximum, yet it is not listed in CISA's KEV catalogue and the record gives no evidence of exploitation in the wild. Applications that rely on the sandbox to safely run untrusted code should not treat that isolation as dependable until it is fixed.

claims.text: CVE-2026-120338 is rated 10.0 (critical) under CVSS 3.1 by the CNA that assigned it.
FIRST's EPSS puts the chance of CVE-2026-120338 being exploited in the next 30 days at 1.2%.

events.title: Northflank Security Incident: Rotate Every Secret, AI Keys First
events.summary: Cloud platform Northflank told customers on 30 October 2026 to assume all environment variables stored on its platform had been decrypted. Customers subsequently reported that AI API keys were involved, though the record does not describe the cause or extent of the incident.
events.why_it_matters: Assuming all stored secrets are exposed means affected customers must rotate credentials, with AI API keys flagged as the priority. The record does not state how many customers were affected or whether keys were actually misused, so impact remains unclear.

events.title: This Box's Admin Was Live, Online, and Actively Trying to Kick Me Out — Red (TryHackMe)
events.summary: A community writeup on DEV Community walks through a medium-difficulty TryHackMe lab machine called Red, where an Apache web server exposes a local file inclusion flaw via its index.php?page= parameter. The walkthrough covers LFI filter bypass techniques, hashcat rule-based password mutation, and privilege escalation using PwnKit.
events.why_it_matters: The record is training content rather than a real incident, but it teaches exploitation of a local file inclusion flaw and PwnKit (CVE-2021-4034), which the record lists as KEV-listed with a CVSS of 7.8 and an EPSS of about 0.95. Defenders reviewing web applications for parameter-driven file inclusion and unpatched legacy systems remain relevant targets for these techniques.

claims.text: CISA lists CVE-2021-4034 as exploited in the wild, added 2022-06-27, with US federal agencies due to fix it by 2022-07-18.
CVE-2021-4034 is rated 7.8 (high) under CVSS 3.1 by CISA in the CVE record.
FIRST's EPSS puts the chance of CVE-2021-4034 being exploited in the next 30 days at 95%.

events.title: OpenAI might rebrand its data centers as ‘AI compute campuses’
events.summary: OpenAI is reportedly considering renaming its data centres to 'AI compute campuses', apparently to counter the facilities' unpopularity. The record offers only this brief speculation from a TechCrunch AI report.

events.summary: Prisoners in Western Australia can buy approved gaming consoles and DVD players for their cells, but the state has officially decided they will not be allowed to play the upcoming Grand Theft Auto VI. The record offers no technical, security or AI dimension — only this policy clarification about entertainment access behind bars.
events.why_it_matters: The record sets out no security implications, vulnerability details, or threat-actor activity. It is a policy story about prisoner entitlements rather than a cyber or AI development, so it offers no actionable guidance for defenders.

events.title: CVSS 10.0 LXD, MicroCloud Flaw Lets Attackers Impersonate Trusted Clients Without a Private Key
events.summary: A critical vulnerability in Canonical's LXD and MicroCloud, rated 10.0, allowed an attacker who could reach the HTTPS API over the network and obtain a trusted client's public certificate to authenticate as that client without the private key. Once impersonated, the attacker could access the cluster and its virtual machines.
events.why_it_matters: A maximum CVSS 10.0 score reflects that network-reachable authentication bypass on cluster management software can hand attackers full control of virtual machine clusters. Defenders running LXD or MicroCloud should prioritise assessing exposure and patching. The record does not state whether exploitation has been observed in the wild or list a CVE.
events.resolution: A critical CVSS 10.0 flaw in Canonical's LXD and MicroCloud allowed attackers who could reach the HTTPS API and obtain a trusted client's public certificate to impersonate that client without its private key, gaining access to the cluster and its virtual machines. The issue was first reported on November 1, 2026, and by November 3 Canonical had released patches to fix it. Organizations running LXD or MicroCloud should apply the updates.

reasons: Global infrastructure software issue with no Australian detail
No Australian organisations or authorities mentioned

events.summary: Attackers tried to exploit a critical remote-code-execution flaw in GitLab to break into Alpine Linux's development infrastructure, prompting the project to rebuild its GitLab server and reset all user passwords as a precaution against possible compromise.

Supply-chain infrastructure like an open-source distro's build systems is attractive to attackers because a compromise could affect downstream users. No CVE or severity details are given in the record.

events.title: SMS of Death: Android under attack, an invisible SMS can block calls and emergency services
events.summary: Researchers describe a zero-click attack called SMS of Death, in which a single crafted SMS message can crash the call-handling service on Android phones, cutting off calls including emergency calls and leaving the device temporarily unusable. No victim interaction is required and no CVEs or severity rating are given in the record.
events.why_it_matters: Because the attack is zero-click and can block emergency calls, a successful message could deny a person phone access at a critical moment. Defenders should note the record gives no CVE, severity score, or evidence of exploitation in the wild, so this is a reported vulnerability without confirmed abuse. Organisations relying on Android handsets for staff communications may want to track vendor patches as they emerge.

events.title: Android SMS of Death Bug Triggers Remote Reboots
events.summary: A critical-severity Android flaw lets malformed WAP Push messages crash telephony services remotely, causing devices to enter persistent boot loops without any user interaction. The record gives no patched versions or affected device details.
events.why_it_matters: The flaw is rated critical and requires no user interaction, meaning a crafted SMS-type message alone can render a phone unusable until remedied. Defenders should track vendor advisories for this telephony issue; the CVE listed in the record (CVE-2026-97406, CVSS 9.1, low EPSS, not KEV-listed) is described there as a separate Bitcoin Core denial-of-service bug, not this Android issue.

claims.text: CVE-2026-97406 is rated 9.1 (critical) under CVSS 3.1 by CISA in the CVE record.

events.title: Rosstat Hack: What Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow Claim, and What Is Confirmed
events.summary: On 1 November 2026 the Belarusian hacktivist groups Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow claimed they had destroyed internal systems of Rosstat, Russia's federal statistics service, and Rosstat reportedly confirmed an incident, though details remain unclear.

events.title: Coincide: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and more, side by side on your Mac
events.summary: A free, open-source Mac app called Coincide lets developers run multiple AI coding agents, including Claude Code, Codex and Cursor, side by side in one window, switching between them mid-task with handover recaps. It runs locally via existing sign-ins or API keys, with nothing routed through its own servers.
events.why_it_matters: This is a developer-workflow tool rather than a security event, but it reduces switching costs between competing AI coding agents, which could shift which tools developers adopt. Its local-only, open-source model is positioned as a privacy-friendly alternative to cloud-mediated tooling.

events.title: The App Blocked Every rockyou.txt Password — So I Built My Own Wordlist From Its Homepage — Silver Platter (TryHackMe)
events.summary: A training walkthrough for the TryHackMe room 'Silver Platter', a medium-difficulty exercise. It covers building a custom password wordlist from a website's own content when common wordlists like rockyou.txt are blocked, plus exploiting an IDOR flaw, finding credentials leaked in a log file, and abusing full sudo rights.
events.why_it_matters: The room highlights that credential-guessing defenses based on blocking well-known wordlists can be bypassed with targeted lists built from public site content, and that exposed log files and IDOR flaws can chain into full compromise.

events.title: Day 43: In-Context Learning Explained
events.summary: An educational post explains in-context learning, where a language model is taught a new task by including examples in the prompt rather than retraining or fine-tuning the model, keeping its parameters unchanged.
events.why_it_matters: The record is educational content with no security angle, breach, vulnerability, or exploitation described. It clarifies that in-context learning changes no model parameters, unlike traditional fine-tuning.

events.title: A File Upload Filter That Had Never Heard of .phtml — RootMe (TryHackMe)
events.summary: A walkthrough of RootMe, an easy TryHackMe lab machine where a web file-upload panel with an incomplete extension filter (missing .phtml) allows a reverse shell, followed by privilege escalation via a Python interpreter running with SUID root.
events.why_it_matters: It is training content, not an incident: the record describes common weaknesses in upload filtering and risky SUID configurations rather than a real-world breach or vulnerability. Defenders can use it to recognise the same patterns in production systems, but the record gives no severity, CVE, or evidence of exploitation.

events.title: 👻 FINDR AI: Unmasking the Ghost in GPS — Intelligent Anomaly Detection & Investigation

The appeal came in a speech marking a 9/11 anniversary.

Defenders responsible for such sites should treat protective security as an expectation from the national security apparatus, not just good practice.

events.title: Building Mintu: A Privacy-First Desktop AI Companion with Tauri 2, Rust, and Local LLMs (v0.2.1 Release)
events.summary: An individual developer has released version 0.2.1 of Mintu, an open-source desktop AI companion built with Tauri 2 and Rust that runs large language models locally on the user's machine and displays as a native overlay on the screen. The project's stated aim is to avoid the privacy drawbacks of cloud-based AI tools and the inconvenience of switching between separate app windows.
events.why_it_matters: This is a software release announcement rather than a security incident. For people choosing AI tools, it illustrates the local-first approach, where model inference happens on-device so data does not leave the machine, though the record presents this as the project's own claim rather than an independently verified safety finding.

events.title: Quoting Kyle Kingsbury
events.summary: A commentary from Kyle Kingsbury, quoted on Simon Willison's blog, argues that large language models make it easier to fake the signals engineers use to judge software quality, undermining trust in documentation and software projects. He questions how maintainers can verify and demonstrate correctness in this environment.
events.why_it_matters: The record raises a trust and verification problem: signs of a mature system, such as accurate documentation, are now easier to counterfeit with generative AI. Defenders and evaluators may need to treat quality signals in new software projects with more suspicion. No specific incident, vulnerability or mitigation is described.

events.title: October 2026 Phishing Report: 144,695 Phished Credentials
events.summary: A threat intelligence vendor reports collecting nearly 145,000 credentials harvested by phishing kits during October 2026, spread across tens of thousands of email addresses and domains. About half were work addresses, and for most of those the stolen passwords did not appear in existing breach or combo lists, meaning they would have been new to credential-monitoring services.
events.why_it_matters: Phishing kit credentials are often missed by breach and combo-list monitoring, so organisations relying on such services may not learn an employee's password was stolen. Roughly 41,000 newly phished work credentials suggest these thefts are not being picked up elsewhere. Defenders are advised to ask their credential monitoring vendors specifically whether they collect phishing-kit passwords.

events.title: Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) in JS & PHP: Spotting Catastrophic Backtracking
events.summary: A community blog post explains how a common JavaScript and PHP regular expression used to validate slugs and usernames can trigger catastrophic backtracking, freezing a Node.js event loop for several seconds on a single crafted input, and walks through spotting such ReDoS patterns.
events.why_it_matters: The record reports measured timings showing one malicious string can stall a single-threaded Node process for about 6.5 seconds, so a handful of parallel requests becomes a denial of service. Defenders should review input-validation regexes, especially slug and username validators, for nested quantifiers that backtrack catastrophically.

events.title: rustgrade: a Rust scanner for the habits coding agents leave behind
events.summary: A developer has released rustgrade, a Rust scanning tool that flags recurring low-quality patterns in code written by AI coding agents, such as unwrap calls, mutexes held across await points, and unnecessary clones.
events.why_it_matters: The record shows that code from coding agents can pass compilation and tests while still containing patterns the author considers undesirable, and that an automated lint-style tool can catch them. For teams using AI-generated Rust, it highlights a verification gap that standard build checks do not cover.

reasons: No Australian connection is mentioned in the record
